# latent_open

Question-tree research pipeline: generate research cards from root questions, check them, and place them in existing
research or industrial programmes. Two runtimes share one script and one set of prompts and gates.

## Layout

- `qt2/src/` pipeline modules (text, schemas, cost, pick, gates, render, prompts, main, replay); `qt2/build.js`
  concatenates them into `qt2/dist/question_tree_v2.js` and `qt2/dist/replay_v2.js`. `qt2/CONTRACT.md` is the spec,
  `qt2/PROMPTS.md` the generated prompt listing, `qt2/tests/` (`node qt2/tests/run.js`).
- `qt2/replay/` args and outputs of the replay and run-F launches (Claude Workflow runtime).
- `qt2/idea/` OpenCode runtime:
  - `wf.js` runs a dist script with every agent call served by an OpenCode model (card generation, full tree, replay).
  - `frame.js` frame check for one card: existing programmes, checked citations, fit scores.
  - `status.js` progress and spend of either kind of run; `oc.js` one OpenCode call; `schema.js` reply checks.
  - `ocx/opencode/opencode.json` the isolated OpenCode config every call runs under (no MCP, deny by default).
  - `config.json` models, timeouts, run directories, OpenCode Go caps.
- `runs/idea/`, `runs/oc/` full logs of OpenCode runs (see below).

## Deployment links

The files live here; the places that load them are symlinks:
- `/home/hal/stage/qt2` -> `qt2/` (Claude Workflow launches and operator prompts use this path)
- `/home/hal/stage/runs-idea`, `/home/hal/stage/runs-oc` -> `runs/idea`, `runs/oc`
- `~/.config/opencode/commands/idea-status.md` -> `qt2/idea/commands/idea-status.md` (`/idea-status` in OpenCode)

Git stores a symlink inside a repo as a link, not the file it points to, so the real file is always the one in this repo.

## Running on OpenCode

```
cd qt2/idea
node wf.js --args seed-I1.json --name I1-card   # card generation (or any dist script via --script)
node frame.js --card R4:interp:I1               # frame check of a run-F card; --card-file for any card
node status.js --latest [--watch]
```

## What a run records

Each `runs/oc/<name>/<stamp>/` holds `run.json` (script hash, args, models, versions, git commit, totals),
`journal.jsonl` (every agent call: started, result with its value, failed, cached; every log line), `status.json`,
`result.json`, `RESULT.md`, and per call `agents/NNNN-<label>/` with `prompt.md` (exact text sent), `events.jsonl`
(OpenCode event stream), `export.json` (`opencode export`: messages, reasoning, tool calls with input and output,
tokens, cost), `reply.txt` and `meta.json`. Frame runs keep `ledger.jsonl`, `raw/` and `research/notes.md` likewise.
Each call also goes through a local logging proxy (`qt2/idea/httplog.js`), so `http/NNN.request.json` holds the exact
provider request (OpenCode's system prompt, tool definitions, messages; credentials redacted) and `NNN.response.txt`
the streamed reply. Passing a session title skips OpenCode's extra title-generation request.

1: # qt2 build contract
2: 
3: Binding for every module agent. Read fully before writing code. Design rationale lives in
4: `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-hal-stage/01679595-7e0a-4a87-9dfe-92f32b9672f2/scratchpad/meta/synthesis/` (INTEGRATED.md, then substrate.md, cost.md, criteria.md, flow.md, options-and-card.md); this file fixes the interfaces. Where this file and a report disagree, this file wins.
5: 
6: ## 0. Decisions from the human (2026-10-16), already applied below
7: 
8: - `require_compute_lever = {physical: true, interp: true}`; gate before producers via `compute_open` status and `sequential` status: ineligible only when both are closed (`compute_open` settled or none, and `sequential` none); a branch with <2 eligible options picks what it has and logs.
9: - `pool_k = 3`. `seed_ideas` (free-text ideas from the human) enter as pool candidates with their own producer, labelled `seed`.
10: - Budget-only constraint: $1,000 at Lambda on-demand list prices. No `max_gpus`, no "one machine", concurrent instances allowed, no FLOP accounting. PRODUCER verbatim prompt loses the words "one machine, up to 8 GPUs,".
11: - Minimal estimates: default cost encoding is time boxes (DESIGN hours × price-sheet rate); `need`, scenarios, yields optional. A GUESS only where a number drives the plan; every load-bearing GUESS/PROXY names the phase that measures it.
12: - Restructuring: `PLAN.restructuring` is required (`method` may be none). Scored by card `reshape` and `baseline`. On restructured plans, `lever` (c) reads "same hardware, method only". (Replaces the optional `PLAN.speedup`, which counted toward `lever` only when it extended the range.)
13: - WIDENER definition suffix: adopted, with a second definition sentence (a problem whose steps run one after another counts, even where more hardware changes only how soon the answer arrives). Writer: render-by-default from producer card fields; WRITER kept as a side cell for the replay comparison. Cost inputs non-blocking in the dramaturg. Payoff shown as dollars at `decides_by`. Credit covers storage, not tax. Reading budget ~25 min; cards for every pick including rejects and halts.
14: - johns-world is the shared 4-core host for producers' local pilots: hang guard in the PRODUCER suffix; every local command under `timeout`.
15: 
16: ## 1. Layout and conventions
17: 
18: ```
19: /home/hal/stage/qt2/
20:   CONTRACT.md            this file
21:   src/text.js            shared text helpers            (owner: gates agent)
22:   src/schemas.js         JSON schemas                   (owner: gates agent)
23:   src/cost.js            numbers, cost evaluation, block (owner: cost agent)
24:   src/pick.js            seeded draws, pick rule         (owner: pick agent)
25:   src/gates.js           gates, decision rule, selftest  (owner: gates agent)
26:   src/render.js          card, table, inventory, result  (owner: render agent)
27:   src/prompts.js         all prompt text, criteria, roles(owner: prompts agent)
28:   src/main.js            workflow script body            (owner: main agent)
29:   src/replay.js          replay workflow script body     (owner: replay agent)
30:   tests/run.js           test runner (given)
31:   tests/<module>.test.js one per module (owner: that module's agent)
32:   tests/fixtures/        copied inputs (each agent copies what it needs, under its own subdir)
33:   tools/                 python helpers for the replay (owner: replay agent)
34:   build.js               (given) concatenates src into dist/
35:   dist/question_tree_v2.js, dist/replay_v2.js   (built; never hand-edited)
36: /home/hal/stage/.claude/agents/qt-*.md          role files (owner: prompts agent)
37: ```
38: 
39: Module rules (the Workflow runtime executes one self-contained plain-JS file; no Node APIs):
40: - Plain script. No `import`, `export`, `require`, `module.exports`. Top-level `function` and `const` only. The build concatenates files in this order: text, schemas, cost, pick, gates, render, prompts, then the main body. `main.js` and `replay.js` must begin with `export const meta = {...}` (a pure literal) followed by the line `// @@MODULES@@`; build.js inserts the modules there.
41: - Names are prefixed by module: `txt_`, `SCHEMA_`, `cost_`, `pick_`, `gate_`, `render_`, `P_` (prompt functions), `CRIT_` (criteria strings), `ROLE_` (role file contents), `ORIG_` (the user's original prompts). No other top-level names.
42: - Forbidden: `Date.now()`, `new Date()` without args, `Math.random()`, filesystem, `console.log` in modules (return logs as arrays). Determinism given `seed`.
43: - A module may call only modules earlier in the build order. `render` may call `cost_render_short`, `cost_render_block`, `cost_render_derivations`, `cost_menu`, `txt_*`. `gates` may call `txt_*`, `cost_*`. `pick` calls `txt_*` only. `main`/`replay` call anything.
44: - Each of cost, pick, gates, render exposes `<prefix>selftest()` returning `{ok: boolean, failures: [string]}` with its planted cases embedded as JS literals. `main` S0 calls all four and returns `{error}` if any fails.
45: - Tests: `node tests/run.js` concatenates `src/*.js` in build order plus every `tests/*.test.js` and runs them in a `vm` context exposing `assert` (node:assert/strict), `test(name, fn)`, and `fixture(relpath)` (returns parsed JSON or text from `tests/fixtures/`). Tests must be pure; no network.
46: - Keep prompt strings free of em-dashes. Write code that reads like the existing script (`/home/hal/.claude/projects/-home-hal-stage/01679595-7e0a-4a87-9dfe-92f32b9672f2/workflows/scripts/question-tree-wf_670c1d45-049.js`): compact, commented where a rule has a reason, no speculative options.
47: 
48: ## 2. Records
49: 
50: All records are returned by agents through the harness `schema` option (JSON Schema, root `type: object`, `required ⊆ properties`). Arrays of items are wrapped as `{items: [...]}`.
51: 
52: ### 2.1 Roots and framer
53: ```
54: QUESTIONS   {items: [{question}]}
55: OVERLAP     {pairs: [{a: rootId, b: rootId, shared_subject}]}          // shared_subject ≥ 3 words
56: VERDICT     {verdict: "COMPUTE-BOUND"|"NOT COMPUTE-BOUND",
57:              compute_signals: [{subproblem, what_compute_buys}]}       // 0..3
58: ```
59: 
60: ### 2.2 Options (branch agents)
61: ```
62: OPTIONS {items: [{ id,            // the heading label used in the branch file
63:                    title, summary,
64:                    root_link,     // one sentence, or "none"
65:                    compute_open,  // one sentence: the quantity more parallel compute would increase here
66:                                   // (samples, ensemble members, resolution, model runs, model size, search width;
67:                                   // interp: models, layers, features, prompts, seeds analysed), where published
68:                                   // measurements of its effect stop with a source URL, and what is unknown above
69:                                   // that; OR "settled: <what is known> <URL>"; OR "none"
70:                    sequential,    // one or two sentences: the chain one answer waits on (what each step waits for, roughly how
71:                                   // many steps), how many independent runs the answer needs, how much of one GPU one run keeps
72:                                   // busy; whether the steps must run in order, and if not, what change would let them run at
73:                                   // the same time, what must be true of the system for that to pay off, and the nearest source
74:                                   // that tried it, with its URL; OR "none: <why the work already splits into independent pieces>"
75:                    source_urls: [str] }]}                              // ≤ 3
76: ```
77: Script derives `compute_open_status`: "settled" if `compute_open` starts with "settled" (case-insensitive), "none" if it equals "none"/"none known" after trim, else "open". Script derives `sequential_status`: "none" if `sequential` starts with "none" (case-insensitive, after trim), else "named". `sequential` is prose: required non-empty (G-opt), never checked for truth. Option key = `${root}:${branch}:${id}`.
78: 
79: ### 2.3 Option critic
80: ```
81: OPTION_SCORES {items: [{ id,
82:                          distance: "SAME"|"ADJACENT"|"ELSEWHERE", distance_reason,
83:                          scores: [{criterion, value: integer 1..5, reason}] }]}   // no NA
84: ```
85: Criteria sets (names are the keys used everywhere): physical `["stakes","open","reshape"]`; interp `["stakes","open","internals","reshape"]`. Totals = sum of the values of every criterion but `reshape` (stakes + open, plus internals for interp), computed by `gate_totals`; `reshape` routes the top pick and the pool and never enters a total, so the open route and the legacy reproduction keep their totals. Script floors (each logged): `compute_open_status` settled/none → the `open` value is overwritten to 1 before totals; `sequential_status` none → the `reshape` value is overwritten to 1 before routing.
86: 
87: ### 2.4 Deduplication and price sheet
88: ```
89: DEDUP       {clusters: [{topic, members: [key]}]}                       // partition of all keys; topic ≥ 3 words
90: PRICE_SHEET {read_at,                                                   // ISO date string from the page fetch, agent-supplied
91:              instances: [{gpu, gpu_memory_gb, n_gpus, per_gpu_usd_h, page_text}],
92:              filesystem: {usd_gib_month, page_text, example: boolean}}
93: ```
94: 
95: ### 2.5 PLAN (producer; also the EXTRACT output)
96: ```
97: PLAN {
98:   option_title,                                  // echoed; gate_plan compares normalised to the pick
99:   question, hypothesis,                          // one sentence each, plain words (card fields)
100:   compute_axis: {quantity, unit, levels: [number]},   // ≥2 levels, max/min ≥ 2
101:   held_fixed: [str],
102:   predictions: {if_lever, if_not,                // card fields; one must contain a digit
103:                 decision_rule,                   // contains a digit
104:                 noise_rule,                      // how a real difference is told from run-to-run noise
105:                 expected: "if_lever"|"if_not"|"unsure", expected_why},
106:   compute_tested: "yes"|"partly"|"no", compute_tested_why,
107:   scored_against,                                // what the measured outcome is compared with
108:   arms: [{id, what}],
109:   baseline: {what, value?, source_id?},
110:   anchor: {what, published_value?, tolerance, source_id?, independent_code?} | {absent_reason},
111:   checks: [str],
112:   phases: [{id, what, stop_rule?, gate?: {on: number_id, op: ">="|"<=", value: number, else: str}}],  // execution order
113:   numbers: [{ id,                                // ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,30}$ ; reserved: budget_usd, fs_usd_gib_month
114:               name, unit,
115:               basis: "CITED"|"PROXY"|"MEASURED"|"DERIVED"|"DESIGN"|"GUESS",
116:               value?,                            // required unless DERIVED
117:               expr?,                             // DERIVED only
118:               source_id?, quote?, page_setting?, // CITED, PROXY
119:               differs_in?: [str],                // PROXY required; MEASURED optional
120:               command?, output?, output_line?, machine?,   // MEASURED; output under <dir>/pilot/
121:               rests_on?,                         // GUESS; free text, no URLs or source ids
122:               measured_by? }],                   // phase id; required when load-bearing GUESS/PROXY
123:   cost: {
124:     rates: [{id, gpu, gpu_memory_gb?, n_gpus, per_gpu_usd_h}],       // checked against the price sheet
125:     lines: [{id, phase, what, kind: "work"|"allotment"|"storage",
126:              rate?, hours?,                      // exprs (string, or a bare number); work/allotment
127:              need?,                              // expr; estimated work when hours is a time box
128:              usd?,                               // expr; storage or dollar allotment
129:              optional?: boolean, instead_of?: [line_id], condition?: str}],
130:     scenarios: [{id, what, set: {number_id: value}}],
131:     yields: [number_id],
132:     spend_cap_usd?,
133:     total_stated: number },
134:   full_scale: [{id, what, usd: expr, ratio_to?: number_id}],
135:   outside_budget: [{what, qty, unit}],
136:   restructuring: {
137:     sequential_part,                             // card field, ≤ 18 words: what one answer waits on step after step, and how many steps
138:     method,                                      // card field, ≤ 22 words: why those steps need not run in order and how the plan
139:                                                  // computes them at the same time; or "none"
140:     condition?,                                  // what must hold about this system for the method to pay off, and the cheap measurement that checks it
141:     condition_phase?,                            // id of the phase that makes that measurement before the main spend
142:     baseline_sequential?,                        // the fastest sequential implementation the plan times, and how it is tuned
143:     baseline_copies? },                          // independent copies run side by side on the same GPUs, which the plan also times
144:   scope_gap: [str],
145:   novelty: {closest_prior,                       // ≤ 30 words: nearest published result and the largest compute amount it used
146:             closest_source_id?, prior_max_level?: number|null,
147:             left_open,                           // ≤ 30 words
148:             decides: "no"|"partly"|"yes",
149:             searched: boolean},
150:   limits: [str],                                 // card field(s)
151:   test_summary,                                  // ≤ 45 words, card field
152:   sources: [{id, url, quote, supports}],
153:   files_read: [str]
154: }
155: ```
156: Card fields (plain words, no record ids as words, caps in words): question 25, hypothesis 22, predictions.if_lever 22, predictions.if_not 25, test_summary 45, novelty.closest_prior 30, novelty.left_open 30, anchor.what 24, limits (joined) 30, restructuring.sequential_part 18, restructuring.method 22. Any card field may cite `[source_id]`.
157: 
158: A plan is "restructured" when `restructuring.method`, trimmed and lowercased, is not "none" (`gate_restructured`). The two restructuring card fields are shown, checked by `gate_cardfields` and sent to the dramaturg only on a restructured plan. On a restructured plan the existing fields carry the rest: `compute_axis` is the chain length or the number of runs the answer needs; `predictions.if_lever`/`if_not` say where on that axis, as numbers, the parallel version does or does not reach the same answer sooner than each baseline (`if_not` names the expected failure); `anchor` checks the parallel result against the sequential one within a tolerance; `test_summary` names both baselines; `novelty.closest_prior` is the nearest published parallel version.
159: 
160: Expression grammar (cost): numbers; ids of numbers, rates (→ instance $/h), lines (→ line $), and the reserved GIVEN ids `budget_usd` and `fs_usd_gib_month` (the price sheet's `filesystem.usd_gib_month`); operators `+ - * / ^ ( )`; functions `ceil floor min max pow`. Literals outside {0, 0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 10, 12, 24, 30, 60, 100, 1000, 1024, 3600, 1e3, 1e6, 1e9, 1e12} are logged as "unlabelled constant". Every expression field (`numbers[].expr`, `lines[].hours/need/usd`, `full_scale[].usd`) accepts a string or a bare number; cost.js reads it through `String()`. A plan may refer to a GIVEN id and may not define it (`reserved` error); the cost block tags both [q]. A plan that uses `fs_usd_gib_month` with no price sheet gets an `undefined` error.
161: 
162: Load-bearing: a number that is an ancestor of any non-optional, non-alternative line's `hours`/`usd`/`need`, any `yields` entry, or any `phases[].gate.on`. Uncertain: load-bearing and (GUESS, or PROXY, or MEASURED with non-empty `differs_in`).
163: 
164: ### 2.6 Dramaturg, critic, repairs
165: ```
166: FINDINGS {items: [{ref, status: "SUPPORTED"|"PARTIAL"|"UNSUPPORTED"|"CONTRADICTED"|"UNREACHABLE", page_quote, note, page_value?: number}]}
167:           // ref ∈ {"card:<field>", "src:<source_id>", "num:<number_id>", "rate:<rate_id>"}
168: CRITIQUE {scores: [{criterion, value: integer 1..5 | "NA", ref, reason}],   // ref: "card:<field>" or "plan:<field path>"
169:           decides_by: phase_id | "none", decides_by_reason}
170: REPAIR_FIELDS {fields: {<field path>: text}}
171: REPAIR_EXPR   {numbers: [{id, expr}], lines: [{id, hours?, usd?, need?}]}
172: ```
173: Card criteria: physical `["stakes","lever","verifiable","open","reshape","baseline"]`; interp `["stakes","lever","verifiable","open","internals","reshape","baseline"]`. `lever` may be "NA" only when `compute_axis` is absent and the branch is exempt (never, under current args; keep the rule). `baseline` may be "NA" only when the plan is not restructured.
174: 
175: Decision rule (`gate_decision`): core refs = `card:question, card:hypothesis, card:test_summary, card:if_lever, card:if_not, card:anchor, card:closest_prior` (plus `card:sequential_part` on a restructured plan) plus every `src:` cited by a core card field. PASS iff no core item is UNSUPPORTED, CONTRADICTED or UNREACHABLE. `num:`/`rate:` items never block; a CONTRADICTED `num:` with `page_value` is re-evaluated as a scenario and blocks only if the plan is then over budget (cost agent exposes `cost_evaluate(plan, given, {overrides})`).

177: ## 3. Module APIs

Module rules (the Workflow runtime executes one self-contained plain-JS file; no Node APIs):

# Learning to Substitute Ingredients in Recipes

Bahare Fatemi Thanks: Work done during an internship at Meta AI (FAIR). Correspondence to: baharef@google.com Affiliation:  Google Research    Quentin Duval Affiliation:  Meta AI    Rohit Girdhar Affiliation:  Meta AI    Michal Drozdzal Affiliation:  Meta AI    Adriana Romero-Soriano Affiliation:  Meta AI

###### Abstract

Recipe personalization through ingredient substitution has the potential to help people meet their dietary needs and preferences, avoid potential allergens, and ease culinary exploration in everyone’s kitchen. To address ingredient substitution, we build a benchmark, composed of a dataset of substitution pairs with standardized splits, evaluation metrics, and baselines. We further introduce Graph-based Ingredient Substitution Module (GISMo), a novel model that leverages the context of a recipe as well as generic ingredient relational information encoded within a graph to rank plausible substitutions. We show through comprehensive experimental validation that GISMo surpasses the best performing baseline by a large margin in terms of mean reciprocal rank. Finally, we highlight the benefits of GISMo by integrating it in an improved image-to-recipe generation pipeline, enabling recipe personalization through user intervention. Quantitative and qualitative results show the efficacy of our proposed system, paving the road towards truly personalized cooking and tasting experiences.

## 1 Introduction

In the current digital era, different food recipes from different cultures and regions in the world are spreading faster than ever. This widespread exposure to different types of cuisines inevitably sparks our interest to try new dishes. Being exposed to this wide variety of foods from different cuisines has widened our horizons and increased, in many cases, our curiosity and willingness to bring the exploration of new recipes home. However, cooking a new dish often requires some degree of recipe personalization due to the potential unavailability of certain ingredients, allergies (*e.g*. to nuts or gluten), personal preferences, or lifestyle. Such recipe personalization usually occurs at the ingredient level, with some ingredients being substituted with alternatives. However, coming up with an ingredient substitution that would maintain the original dish taste as closely as possible is not trivial and requires broad cooking knowledge, as one ingredient might need to be substituted with different alternatives when appearing in different recipes. For example, *applesauce* may be a good substitute for *oil* when baking a cake but may not be as well suited when frying chicken. Overall, recipe personalization via ingredient substitution has the potential to improve our culinary experiences by helping us avoid ingredients that might be expensive, rare, allergic, or outside our dietary preferences.

![Refer to caption](/html/2302.07960/assets/teaser.png)

Figure 1: Overview of personalized image-to-recipe generation system with ingredient substitution. Given an ingredient to substitute, our ingredient substitution model, GISMo, suggests an alternative ingredient. The set of ingredients is updated and then used together with the image to generate the personalized recipe.

Most existing approaches to ingredient substitution are based on information extracted from textual recipes, including simple statistics – *e.g*. Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency [shidochi2009finding](#bib.bib53); [boscarino2014automatic](#bib.bib3); [yamanishi2015alternative](#bib.bib60) –, and ingredient co-occurrences [achananuparp2016extracting](#bib.bib1); [morales2021word](#bib.bib39); [lawo2020veganaizer](#bib.bib31); [kazama2018neural](#bib.bib29). Only recently, researchers have started to explore advances in natural language processing (NLP) – *e.g*. word2vec [word2vec](#bib.bib38), BERT [devlin2018bert](#bib.bib13), and R-BERT [wu2019enriching](#bib.bib58) – to obtain ingredient embeddings [foodbert](#bib.bib45); [shirai2020identifying](#bib.bib54), showing the benefits of representation learning to improve the task of ingredient substitution. This has been further emphasized with the development of node embedding methods to learn ingredient substitutions from the recently introduced large-scale FlavorGraph of ingredient relations and flavor molecules [park2021flavorgraph](#bib.bib43). However, all the above-mentioned methods assume that ingredients have universal substitutions that are suitable in the context of any recipe. Moreover, obtaining high-quality ingredient substitutions is not sufficient to personalize recipes, since substituted ingredients oftentimes require adapting the cooking instructions. For example, when baking a cake, we may want to use *banana* instead of *egg*. However, the way to process eggs – *whisk eggs* – is different from the way to process bananas – *mash bananas*. Therefore, learning-based approaches have been further extended in [li2021share](#bib.bib33) to not only propose ingredient substitutions but also alter the cooking instructions accordingly. This has been achieved by introducing a fully supervised pipeline that assumes access to pairs of original and personalized recipes, which are rather rare to find at scale and which are unfortunately not made publicly available.

Therefore, in this paper, we decouple the ingredient substitution from the recipe editing task, and instead, we focus on extracting ingredient substitution pairs from the flurry of readily accessible user comments found on recipe websites. As a result, we create a benchmark for ingredient substitutions called Recipe1MSubs, with substitution pairs associated with the Recipe1M dataset [recipe1m](#bib.bib51) recipes. Our benchmark contains a dataset of valid ingredient substitution pairs together with their corresponding recipes as well as standardized dataset splits and metrics.

Moreover, we introduce Graph-based Ingredient Substitution Module (GISMo), a novel ingredient substitution model which leverages not only the substitution context from a recipe but also generic ingredient relational information found in a large corpus of recipes, available through the FlavorGraph. More precisely, GISMo leverages recent advances in graph neural networks (GNNs) to capture common ingredient interactions within the learned ingredient embeddings, which are then updated with contextual information from a given recipe to predict plausible ingredient substitutions. We extensively evaluate our model and compare it with baselines, showing a performance improvement of ~14% in mean reciprocal rank over the best performing approach, and highlighting the value of leveraging complementary recipe-specific and generic ingredient relational information.

Finally, we plug GISMo into the inverse cooking system from [salvador2019inverse](#bib.bib49) to enable recipe editing. Inverse cooking first predicts the set of ingredients in an image and then generates a cooking recipe from the predicted ingredients and the input image. We modify the pipeline such that predicted ingredients are fed to GISMo together with a mask indicating the ingredient to be substituted, as specified by the user. The resulting updated set of ingredients is used along the input image to generate the edited recipe, leveraging the compositionality captured by language models to operate outside of training distribution at inference time as opposed to requiring full supervision to generate personalized recipes. We further improve this pipeline by taking advantage of a vision transformer (ViT) [dosovitskiy2021an](#bib.bib15) backbone to predict the ingredients in the input image. Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Learning to Substitute Ingredients in Recipes") depicts the proposed personalized inverse cooking pipeline.

The contributions of this paper can be summarized as:

-   •
    
    We create Recipe1MSubs, a benchmark for ingredient substitution.
    
-   •
    
    We develop GISMo, a novel GNN-based ingredient substitution model, which leverages both recipe-specific context and generic ingredient relations to predict and rank plausible substitutes and improves upon previous approaches by a large margin.
    
-   •
    
    We extend the inverse cooking pipeline [salvador2019inverse](#bib.bib49) by enabling recipe personalization and show through extensive evaluation that the generated recipes effectively incorporate the modifications suggested by GISMo.
    

Code for the personalized inverse cooking pipeline and the benchmark Recipe1MSubs available at [https://github.com/facebookresearch/gismo](https://github.com/facebookresearch/gismo).

## 2 Ingredient substitution benchmark

Ingredient substitution task. The goal of ingredient substitution is to propose a valid substitution for a given ingredient in a recipe. Each recipe, rr, is composed of a title, tt, a set of ingredients, ℐ\\mathcal{I}, and a list of preparation instructions, P. During ingredient substitution, we modify the set of ingredients ℐ\\mathcal{I} and update it into ℐ′\\mathcal{I^{\\prime}} with the substituted ingredient, assuming that an ingredient may be replaced by a single ingredient. More precisely, given an ingredient vocabulary 𝒟i​n​g{\\mathcal{D}\_{ing}} containing all ingredients in all recipes, the objective is to substitute a source ingredient s∈𝒟i​n​gs\\in{\\mathcal{D}\_{ing}} for a target ingredient y∈𝒟i​n​gy\\in{\\mathcal{D}\_{ing}} such that ℐ′\=ℐ∖{s}∪{y}\\mathcal{I^{\\prime}}=\\mathcal{I}\\setminus\\{s\\}\\cup\\{y\\}. We call (s,y)(s,y) a *substitution tuple*. It is worth noting that substitution tuples are directional and may only be valid given the *context* of the recipe. Therefore, we assume that we have access to a large dataset of JJ recipes and substitution tuples τ\={(s,y)j,rj}j\=1j\=J\\tau=\\{(s,y)\_{j},r\_{j}\\}\_{j=1}^{j=J}, and denote as τt​r​a​i​n\\tau\_{train}, τv​a​l\\tau\_{val}, and τt​e​s​t\\tau\_{test} its respective training, validation and test splits.

Ingredient substitution dataset. Recipe1M [recipe1m](#bib.bib51) is the largest publicly available collection of recipe data composed of 1,029,7201,\\!029,\\!720 recipes scraped from cooking websites. It contains 720,639720,\\!639 training, 155,036155,\\!036 validation and 154,045154,\\!045 test recipes, with a title, a set of ingredients, a list of cooking instructions and (optionally) an image. However, this dataset does not contain ingredient substitution information. Inspired by [foodbert](#bib.bib45), we crawled the Recipe1M recipe websites, identified all comments in the recipes, and extracted all sentences in the comments containing keywords potentially related to substitutions: “instead”, “substitute”, “in place of” and “replace”. Next, we filtered the phrases containing substitution keywords as follows:

-   •
    
    We kept phrases that contain exactly two ingredients, as a different number of ingredients in the same sentence might not reflect a valid substitution.
    
-   •
    
    We kept phrases where the ingredients and substitution keywords are not *far away* from each other to ensure keywords refer to the substitution (a distance of ≥7\\geq 7 is considered as *far away*, value set by visual inspection).
    
-   •
    
    We kept phrases where *only* one of the two identified ingredients is part of the original recipe ingredient set and store just the ingredient substitution pair by dropping all non-ingredients from the phrase.
    

As a result, we obtain Recipe1MSubs dataset that enables benchmarking models for the ingredient substitution problem. Each data point in Recipe1MSubs contains a substitution tuple (s,y)(s,y), as well as the recipe ID (from the Recipe1M dataset) for which the substitution is valid. Using the recipe IDs and following the Recipe1M dataset ID splits, we get 49,04449,\\!044, 10,72910,\\!729 and 10,74710,\\!747 substitution samples for training, validation, and test sets respectively.

Evaluation metrics. We follow the literature on recommender systems and link predictors on graphs [pinsage](#bib.bib61); [transe](#bib.bib2); [simple-plus](#bib.bib17) and evaluate the ingredient substitution task with Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) and Hit@kk, k∈{1,3,10}k\\in\\{1,3,10\\}. Both MRR and Hit@kk rely on *ranking* the ingredients in 𝒟i​n​g∖{s}{\\mathcal{D}\_{ing}}\\setminus\\{s\\} for each recipe and source ingredient. The MRR computes the multiplicative inverse of the rank of the correct substitution answer, as determined by yy. Hit@kk measures the proportion of correct substitutions that rank among the top kk answers. However, since there are cases for which different substitutions (target ingredients) might be proposed for the same source ingredient within a recipe, we avoid penalizing for such cases through their ranking by accepting all valid target ingredients as correct answers at evaluation time.

## 3 GISMo

Given the context recipe rr and an ingredient to be substituted ss, the objective of GISMo is to predict the target ingredient yy to use as a substitution. GISMo consists of three components: 1) an ingredient encoder, 2) a context encoder, and 3) an ingredient substitution decoder. See Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 GISMo ‣ Learning to Substitute Ingredients in Recipes") for an illustration of the pipeline.

Ingredient encoder (IE\\mathrm{IE}). This module takes as input a matrix of ingredient features as well as a graph structure – represented using an adjacency matrix – capturing ingredient relations and producing an embedding for each ingredient in the graph. The encoder is built from an optional embedding layer – required when the ingredient features are one-hot encodings of the ingredients in 𝒟i​n​g{\\mathcal{D}\_{ing}} –, followed by multiple Graph Isomorphism Network (GIN) [gin](#bib.bib59) layers, given their properties, high performance, and ubiquitous use in the literature [hu2021open](#bib.bib26). Each GIN layer is defined as follows:

## 4 Personalized inverse cooking pipeline

To enable recipe personalization, we integrate GISMo in the inverse cooking pipeline described in [salvador2019inverse](#bib.bib49) and introduce the *personalized inverse cooking pipeline*. Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3 GISMo ‣ Learning to Substitute Ingredients in Recipes") illustrates the full pipeline at inference time. First, an image is fed to the image encoder and an image embedding is obtained. The image embedding is then used to predict a set of ingredients. GISMo module acts on the predicted ingredient set and substitutes one selected ingredient specified by the user. Next, the ingredient encoder of inverse cooking takes as an input the modified ingredient set and produces ingredient embeddings. Finally, both the ingredient embeddings of the modified ingredient set as well as the image embedding are fed into a recipe decoder that outputs a generated and personalized recipe. Important modifications w.r.t. [salvador2019inverse](#bib.bib49) include the image encoder architecture, where we swap ResNet [HeZRS15](#bib.bib24) for Vision Transformers (ViT) [dosovitskiy2021an](#bib.bib15). We further extend the ViT architecture by concatenating features corresponding to odd layers’ outputs in the classification token as it proved to perform slightly better in our experiments than the vanilla ViT architecture. We refer to this modified ViT architecture as ViT Multi Layer Sequence, ViT MLS. Moreover, in contrast to [salvador2019inverse](#bib.bib49) and as suggested in [Pineda-1904](#bib.bib46) we train our image encoder using the binary cross-entropy loss. At training time, we remove the GISMo module and train the pipeline following the inverse cooking approach. Thus, at inference time, the personalized inverse cooking pipeline operates out of training distribution.

## 5 Experiments

In this section, we evaluate GISMo and the personalized inverse cooking pipeline. We start by providing experimental details, followed by results and ablations of both models.

### 5.1 Experimental details

Relations between ingredients. To represent the relations between ingredients we use FlavorGraph [park2021flavorgraph](#bib.bib43). FlavorGraph is a graph of ingredient relations extracted from Recipe1M [recipe1m](#bib.bib51), which models ingredient co-occurrences in recipes. The graph also incorporates flavor molecules associated with the ingredients. In particular, it contains 6,6536,\\!653 food ingredient nodes and 1,6451,\\!645 flavor molecule (or chemical compound) nodes. Edges between two ingredient nodes reflect their association, computed as their normalized point-wise mutual information [bouma2009normalized](#bib.bib6). Edges between ingredients and chemical compounds capture the chemical compounds in a food ingredient. Future work can study whether structure learning techniques [idgl](#bib.bib12); [fatemi2021slaps](#bib.bib16) can identify latent structures between ingredients that help the task.

Ingredient vocabulary. Since FlavorGraph contains a subset of ingredients from Recipe1M, we process the ingredients in Recipe1M and Recipe1MSubs such that they match those in FlavorGraph, *e.g*. by merging singulars and plurals, different spellings of the same ingredient, or very infrequent ingredients with their closest match. As a result, our ingredient vocabulary contains 6,6536,\\!653 ingredients. Note that the original inverse cooking pipeline [salvador2019inverse](#bib.bib49) uses a pre-processed vocabulary of 1,4881,\\!488 ingredients, which is more than 4×4\\times smaller than the FlavorGraph-based one.

GISMo details. We implement our model in PyTorch [paszke2017automatic](#bib.bib44), and use deep graph library (DGL) [wang2019deep](#bib.bib57) for the sparse operations. We use the Adam [adam](#bib.bib30) optimizer, and perform early stopping and hyperparameter tuning based on the MRR on the validation set in all cases. We defer more details to the supplementary material.

Personalized inverse cooking pipeline details. We train our pipeline following [salvador2019inverse](#bib.bib49). We start by training the image-to-ingredient prediction module, and then train the recipe generator using teacher forcing both from the ground truth ingredients and recipe. We add weight decay in the recipe generation training stage, as we found it helped mitigate the overfitting caused by the increased number of ingredients in our vocabulary. The weight decay was set to 10−510^{-5} after a sweep among \[0.0,10−6,10−5,10−4,10−3\]\[0.0,10^{-6},10^{-5},10^{-4},10^{-3}\]. Note that GISMo is trained on its own and only used at inference time within the pipeline.

### 5.2 Evaluating GISMo

Baselines. We consider the following statistical, language model-based, and graph-based baselines. Random: This baseline randomly ranks all possible ingredient substitutions given a source ingredient and a recipe. Mode: This baseline finds the ingredient that appears the most often as a target ingredient across all data samples in τt​r​a​i​n\\tau\_{train}, and uses it as a proposed substitution in all cases. Lookup table (LT): For each source ingredient, this baseline assigns rank 1 to all target ingredients that appear together with said source ingredient in the substitution tuples of τt​r​a​i​n\\tau\_{train}. Frequency (Freq): This baseline counts the number of times each v∈𝒟i​n​gv\\in{\\mathcal{D}\_{ing}} is suggested as a target ingredient in τt​r​a​i​n\\tau\_{train}, and uses these frequencies to rank ingredient substitutions. Lookup table + Frequency (LT+freq): This baseline combines the LT and Freq ranking approaches and computes how often a target ingredient appears for each source ingredient in τt​r​a​i​n\\tau\_{train}. Those frequencies are then used to rank ingredient substitutions for each source ingredient. Food2Vec, FoodBERT, and R-FoodBERT: Those are language model-based approaches introduced in [foodbert](#bib.bib45). Food2Vec and FoodBERT finetune respectively word2vec [word2vec](#bib.bib38) and BERT [devlin2018bert](#bib.bib13) models on cooking instructions of the Recipe1M dataset, and then use the updated word embeddings to suggest ingredients substitutions. The assumption is that ingredients that are close to each other in the embedding space are good candidate substitutions for each other. R-FoodBERT further finetunes the FoodBERT model on user comments crawled from the Recipe1M recipe websites, which contain substitution information. Metapath2vec [park2021flavorgraph](#bib.bib43): This baseline implicitly learns structural node embeddings by leveraging the metapath2vec [metapath2vec](#bib.bib14), an extension of node2vec [grover2016node2vec](#bib.bib21) that operates on graphs with different node types. The approach enhances the node embedding learning of metapath2vec by including chemical property information.

Results. Results are averaged over 5 runs and are reported in Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5.1 Experimental details ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Learning to Substitute Ingredients in Recipes"). The strongest statistical approach is LT+Freq, which is a combination of LT and Freq baselines, and achieves an MRR score of 27.6627.66. We can also see that using LT and Freq on their own leads in both cases to relatively poor MRR scores. Among the language model baselines, R-FoodBERT performs the best, reaching 10.0910.09 MRR score. However, none of the language model baselines outperforms the LT+Freq baseline, suggesting that direct access to ingredient substitution tuples is beneficial. When it comes to node embeddings learned from random walks on the graph (metapath2vec), results drop by a large margin and are among the weakest ones. This is perhaps unsurprising given that FlavorGraph captures ingredient co-occurrences but has no direct information about plausible ingredient substitutions. To assess the importance of leveraging the information captured by FlavorGraph in a more explicit way and in the context of ingredient substitution, we borrow a model from the GNN-based recommender system literature and simplify it to fit our task. The simplification comes from the absence of user-item interactions in our data. The model [pinsage](#bib.bib61), PinSAGE, leverages GraphSAGE [NIPS2017\_Hamilton](#bib.bib22) layers to learn node embeddings through a max-margin ranking loss. The learned embeddings are then used to suggest ingredient substitutions through nearest neighbor lookups. As shown in the table, PinSAGE outperforms all the language model-based approaches, with an MRR of 17.8617.86, suggesting that the generic ingredient relational information captured by the FlavorGraph is useful11 1 We also tested a variant of PinSAGE with GIN layers and observed that the results were unaffected.. However, the approach still falls far behind the LT+Freq baseline. Finally, we notice that our model can outperform all alternative approaches, improving the MRR score by 14%14\\% w.r.t. the LT+Freq baseline. Similar trends hold for the Hit@ metrics, with GISMo consistently outperforming other methods.

To gain further understanding of models’ behavior, we report the MRR score on the stratified dataset in Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Evaluating GISMo ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Learning to Substitute Ingredients in Recipes"). Leveraging the graph structure of FlavorGraph enables node ingredients in OOD tuples to update their embeddings through messages from their neighbors in the GNN forward pass. Figure 4: Example of a personalized recipe. The image of a “beer bread loaf” is fed to the inverse cooking pipeline. We then ask to substitute *beer* and GISMo suggests using *water* instead. The generated recipe is entitled by the model as “whole wheat bread”. Next, we evaluate the effect of GISMo on the quality of the generated recipes. As we do not have ground truth recipes with the modified ingredient set, we rely on multiple complementary metrics to judge the quality of generated recipes. First, we consider the perplexity of personalized recipes from modified ingredients w.r.t. the ground truth recipe (PPL). We compare the personalized recipes, both from ground truth substitutions and predicted substitutions, to the ones generated from the original ground truth ingredients to determine how much the personalized recipes deviate from the non-personalized ones. Second, we compute the perplexity of the generated recipes w.r.t. a pretrained GPT2-medium [radford2019language](#bib.bib48) (GPT2 PPL) to further assess the quality of the generated recipes, following  [Zhang\*2020BERTScore:](#bib.bib62); [BLEURT\_Sellam](#bib.bib52). The GPT2 PPL metric is obtained by concatenating the generated recipes to an initial prompt ”recipe instructions:” which serves as a context for GPT2 to switch to a *recipe world*. As GPT2 has been shown to be sensitive to text features such as text length [miaschi-etal-2021-makes](#bib.bib37), we complement the metric by reporting the average length of the generated recipes, and the number of unique vocabulary words in them. These metrics help us identify potential short and non-specific generations such as “mix all ingredients”. Finally, we include the intersection over union (IoU) to measure the consistency between the ingredients used as a conditioning and those appearing in the generated recipes. However, since the recipes often contain ambiguous references to the ingredients such as *pepper* to refer to *cayenne pepper* or *dry ingredients* to refer to a bunch of dry ingredients all together, the results of this metric should be interpreted as a rough indication of consistency. We complete our analysis with a qualitative evaluation of the generated recipe by visual inspections.

The results for this experiment are reported in Table [6](#S5.T6 "Table 6 ‣ 5.4 Personalized inverse cooking evaluation ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Learning to Substitute Ingredients in Recipes"), which shows average metrics for 25 models obtained by changing random seed (5 runs of the GISMo model and 5 runs of the inverse cooking one). The table measures the effect of ingredient substitutions on the quality of the generated recipes. In particular, it contrasts the effect of introducing no substitutions, with substitutions coming from the ground truth tuples of Recipe1MSubs, the substitutions predicted by GISMo, as well as random substitutions. Based on the results, we can conclude that the inverse cooking pipeline does not deviate too much from the generated recipe when we substitute the ground truth ingredients and maintains ingredient consistency in the generated recipes as indicated by the IoU metric. Recipes generated with substitutions do not increase the number of non-specific recipes – *i.e*., the ingredient IoU stays within standard deviation for all three tested scenarios and the recipe length is also approximately maintained, suggesting that leveraging the compositionality captured by language models is a good alternative to collecting supervised recipe pairs when it comes to recipe editing. When it comes to random substitution, we observe an expected increase in PPL and a decrease in IoU w.r.t. other substitution strategies. However, the GPT2 PPL does not appear to be affected (within std).

Finally, we report a qualitative result in Figure [4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 5.4 Personalized inverse cooking evaluation ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Learning to Substitute Ingredients in Recipes"). One can observe that the GISMo module proposes a reasonable substitution in this case – suggesting to use *water* instead of *beer* –, and that the generated recipe reflects well the changes in the personalized recipe. When comparing the personalized recipe to the recipe obtained by the inverse cooking pipeline, we observe that the substitution proposed by GISMo affected only one cooking instruction and modified the recipe title, changing it from *beer bread* to *whole wheat bread*.

## 6 Related work

Food understanding. Food understanding has been gaining momentum in the computer vision community since the introduction of large-scale datasets [bossard2014food](#bib.bib4). The researchers have investigated a variety of food-related recognition tasks, such as image classification [horiguchi2018personalized](#bib.bib25); [lee2018cleannet](#bib.bib32), ingredient classification [chen2017cross](#bib.bib8), calorie estimation [Meyers\_2015\_ICCV](#bib.bib36) quantity prediction [chen2012automatic](#bib.bib9), and food question answering [FoodQA](#bib.bib11). More recently, the inception of Recipe1M dataset [marin2019recipe1m+](#bib.bib35) triggered the research in cross-modal recipe retrieval [Retrieval\_Lien](#bib.bib34); [Zhu\_2019\_CVPR](#bib.bib64); [salvador2021revamping](#bib.bib50), image-to-recipe generation [salvador2019inverse](#bib.bib49); [SAGN\_Wang](#bib.bib56); [nishimura-etal-2019-procedural](#bib.bib40); [chandu-etal-2019-storyboarding](#bib.bib7) as well as recipe-to-image generation [ChefGAN](#bib.bib41); [CookGANZhu\_2020\_CVPR](#bib.bib63); [CookGANHan](#bib.bib23). It is worth noting that topics of food understanding have also been explored in the natural language processing literature, where significant effort has been devoted to advancing recipe generation [NLP\_Pan](#bib.bib42); [NLP\_singh](#bib.bib55), and food recommendation systems [jiang2019market2dish](#bib.bib27).

Ingredient substitution and recipe editing. The vast amount of cooking recipes available online has triggered the exploration of ingredient substitution methods which leverage textual information. In particular, [shidochi2009finding](#bib.bib53); [boscarino2014automatic](#bib.bib3); [yamanishi2015alternative](#bib.bib60) have applied statistical methods such as Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency on recipe instructions to propose valid ingredient substitution. Similarly, recipe editing has been studied by leveraging ingredient co-occurrences [achananuparp2016extracting](#bib.bib1); [morales2021word](#bib.bib39); [shirai2020identifying](#bib.bib54); [lawo2020veganaizer](#bib.bib31); [kazama2018neural](#bib.bib29) to meet dietary restrictions and adapt recipes to regional cuisines. More recently, researchers have leveraged recent advances in the natural language processing literature – *e.g*., word2vec [word2vec](#bib.bib38), BERT [devlin2018bert](#bib.bib13), and R-BERT [wu2019enriching](#bib.bib58) – to learn ingredient embeddings from recipe instructions and/or user comments [foodbert](#bib.bib45). The learned embeddings are then used in the context of ingredient substitution by applying the kk\-nearest neighbors algorithm [fix1951discriminatory](#bib.bib20). Moreover, [li2021share](#bib.bib33) has tackled the problem of recipe editing by collecting pairs of original and edited recipes. Finally, the introduction of a large-scale graph of ingredient co-occurrences and food molecules, the FlavorGraph [park2021flavorgraph](#bib.bib43), has triggered the exploration of node embedding methods. In particular, metapath2vec [metapath2vec](#bib.bib14); [park2021flavorgraph](#bib.bib43) has been extended to incorporate chemical properties, and as a result, improve food pairing.

## 7 Discussion

Conclusions. In this paper, we tackled the problem of recipe personalization by decoupling ingredient substitution from recipe editing. We addressed ingredient substitution by introducing a benchmark for the task. We then devised a graph-based ingredient substitution module able to leverage recipe-specific context and generic ingredient relational information encoded as a graph simultaneously to predict plausible substitutions. Finally, we took advantage of the compositionality captured by pretrained language models to integrate the proposed ingredient substitution model within the inverse cooking pipeline, and highlighted the effectiveness of the system to come up with plausible substitutions and adequate recipe modifications. Our research takes one step forward to increase creativity in everyone’s kitchen through personalized tasting experiences.

Limitations. We consider a single ingredient substitution. Although this setup works well in our experiments, the users might want to substitute multiple ingredients at once. Moreover, by design we always consider one-to-one substitutions, meaning that a single source ingredient can be substituted by one target ingredient. This might be unrealistic in some scenarios, where a single ingredient should be substituted by multiple ingredients. Future work can study whether learning with hypergraphs (*e.g*.  [feng2019hypergraph](#bib.bib19); [knowledge-hypergraphs](#bib.bib18)) can help with many-to-many substitutions.

Potential negative societal impact. Our work is based on the Recipe1M dataset that was scraped from mostly US-centric food webpages. Thus, as a result, the learned substitutions might have a bias toward western cuisines, and the system might not work equally well for everyone.

# Title:Optimizing Ingredient Substitution Using Large Language Models to Enhance Phytochemical Content in Recipes

Authors:[Luis Rita](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Rita,+L), [Josh Southern](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Southern,+J), [Ivan Laponogov](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Laponogov,+I), [Kyle Higgins](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Higgins,+K), [Kirill Veselkov](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Veselkov,+K)

View a PDF of the paper titled Optimizing Ingredient Substitution Using Large Language Models to Enhance Phytochemical Content in Recipes, by Luis Rita and 3 other authors

[View PDF](/pdf/2409.08792)

> Abstract:In the emerging field of computational gastronomy, aligning culinary practices with scientifically supported nutritional goals is increasingly important. This study explores how large language models (LLMs) can be applied to optimize ingredient substitutions in recipes, specifically to enhance the phytochemical content of meals. Phytochemicals are bioactive compounds found in plants, which, based on preclinical studies, may offer potential health benefits. We fine-tuned models, including OpenAI's GPT-3.5, DaVinci, and Meta's TinyLlama, using an ingredient substitution dataset. These models were used to predict substitutions that enhance phytochemical content and create a corresponding enriched recipe dataset. Our approach improved Hit@1 accuracy on ingredient substitution tasks, from the baseline 34.53 plus-minus 0.10% to 38.03 plus-minus 0.28% on the original GISMo dataset, and from 40.24 plus-minus 0.36% to 54.46 plus-minus 0.29% on a refined version of the same dataset. These substitutions led to the creation of 1,951 phytochemically enriched ingredient pairings and 1,639 unique recipes. While this approach demonstrates potential in optimizing ingredient substitutions, caution must be taken when drawing conclusions about health benefits, as the claims are based on preclinical evidence. Future work should include clinical validation and broader datasets to further evaluate the nutritional impact of these substitutions. This research represents a step forward in using AI to promote healthier eating practices, providing potential pathways for integrating computational methods with nutritional science.

# Palm Oil Fact Sheet

Palm oil is a globally traded agricultural commodity that is used in 50 percent of all consumer goods, from lipstick and packaged food to body lotion and biofuels.\[1\] Used in about half of the products on supermarket shelves, palm oil imports to the U.S. have jumped 485% in the last decade, \[2\]pushing palm oil cultivation into the rainforests and making this crop one of the key causes of rainforest destruction around the globe.

Approximately 85 percent of palm oil is grown in the tropical countries of Indonesia, Malaysia and Papua New Guinea (PNG) on industrial plantations \[3\] that have severe impacts on the environment, forest peoples and the climate.

## Palm oil destroys rainforests

Indonesia’s tropical rainforests are among the world’s most diverse. They provide critical habitat to species including highly endangered Sumatran tigers, Sumatran elephants and orangutans. The Indonesian government has announced plans to convert approximately 18 million more hectares of rainforests, an area the size of Missouri, into palm oil plantations by 2020.\[4\]

## Palm oil threatens forest peoples

Tens of millions of Indonesians rely directly on rainforests for their livelihoods.\[5\] A single palm oil plantation can destroy the forests, watersheds, and forest resources of thousands of Indonesians, leaving entire forest communities to face poverty, many for the first time.\[6\]

## Palm oil causes climate change

Rainforests are the earth’s largest sinks of carbon, safely storing the greenhouse gases that cause climate change. In Indonesia, rainforests are razed to create industrial palm oil plantations, releasing massive quantities of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.\[7\] In fact, deforestation causes eighty percent of Indonesia’s CO2 emissions, making the tropical nation the world’s third largest emitter of greenhouse gases.\[8\]

## Who is responsible?

North American food and agribusiness companies purchase from, operate, and own many palm oil plantations in Southeast Asia, making our corporations a powerful force in the palm oil market.

The largest privately owned company in the U.S.,\[10\] Cargill dominates the American palm oil market. They own five palm oil plantations in Indonesia and PNG and are the largest importer of palm oil into the U.S., sourcing from at least 26 producers and buying roughly 11 percent of Indonesia’s total oil palm output.\[11\] A large and growing number of investigations have shown that Cargill’s palm oil is directly destroying forests, eliminating biodiversity and harming forest peoples.\[12\]

RAN is actively working to stop the destruction of rainforests due to industrial agribusiness expansion. We encourage companies like Cargill  to stop producing, trading and purchasing palm oil that destroys rainforests using grassroots pressure, corporate engagement, and non-violent direct action.

# PLAN — FD1: Industrial food ingredient replacement for sustainability

Working file for the producer. The machine-readable record is returned separately.

## Option

- id: FD1
- title: Industrial food ingredient replacement for sustainability
- root question: "Industrial food ingredient replacement for sustainability? Industrial food recipe replacement for sustainability?"
- seed idea from notes; compute_open / sequential not given.

## What to build

A neural **ingredient-substitution ranker** trained on the public **Recipe1MSubs** benchmark
(Fatemi et al. 2023, arXiv:2302.07960, code at github.com/facebookresearch/gismo). Given a
recipe context and a source ingredient, it scores every ingredient in a fixed 6,653-ingredient
vocabulary and ranks them; the correct substitute should rank high. Metric: **MRR and Hit@1/3/10**
on the 10,747-sample test split.

The test varies the ranker's **embedding width** (64 / 128 / 256 / 512), i.e. model capacity,
and measures whether Hit@1 keeps rising. This is the compute lever: a wider encoder costs more
FLOPs and GPU memory per step, so more GPUs buy the larger widths.

Sustainability tie-in: the benchmark's substitutions cover high-footprint ingredients (butter,
egg, milk, cream, beef, pork, chicken, cheese, oil). The final (optional) phase re-evaluates the
best width on the test tuples whose source ingredient is in a curated high-footprint list, which
is exactly the "replace this ingredient for sustainability" use case. Stakes: palm oil alone is
used in 50% of consumer goods (RAN) and food is ~90% of palm-oil use (Riau/PLOS ONE).

## Baseline and anchor

- Baseline to beat (non-neural): LT+Freq, MRR 27.66, Hit@1 18.10 (Table 1 of the GISMo paper).
- Anchor to reproduce first: GISMo test MRR 31.51, Hit@1 20.56 (Table 1), averaged over 5 runs.
  Reproduce with the official gismo code within ±2.0 MRR points before spending on the sweep.

## How to check it is right

1. Downloaded splits match 49,044 / 10,729 / 10,747 samples.
2. Ranking is over the 6,653-ingredient vocabulary, matching GISMo.
3. Anchor mean MRR lands within 2 points of 31.51 (else the pipeline is wrong; stop).
4. Each width averaged over 5 seeds; a real effect exceeds twice the pooled std (GISMo's Hit@1 std is 0.14).
5. Decision rule: Hit@1(width 512) − Hit@1(width 64) ≥ 2.0 points and > 2× pooled std → compute is the lever.

## Compute axis

quantity: substitution-ranker capacity (ingredient-encoder embedding width)
unit: dimension
levels: [64, 128, 256, 512]

held fixed: Recipe1MSubs benchmark + test split; FlavorGraph + 6,653 vocabulary; contrastive
loss, Adam, early stopping on validation MRR; 5 seeds per width; MRR/Hit@k metrics.

## Predictions

- if_lever: Hit@1 rises with width, reaching at least 22% at width 512 (above GISMo's 20.56), and still climbing.
- if_not: Hit@1 plateaus near GISMo's 20.56 at every width; wider models are not the lever.
- expected: if_lever — published LLM fine-tuning lifted Hit@1 on this benchmark family (34.53 → 38.03), so capacity should help.

## Cost (Lambda on-demand, price sheet read 2026-10-17)

- r_a100_1: 1× NVIDIA A100 SXM 40GB, $1.99/GPU/h
- r_a100_4: 4× NVIDIA A100 PCIe 40GB, $1.99/GPU/h (instance $7.96/h)

method: none (independent model widths/seeds run side by side; each batch splits across the 4 GPUs).

- src_gismo_vocab (arXiv:2302.07960): "our ingredient vocabulary contains 6,653 ingredients."
